content: Poor nutrition is a common issue in individuals with cystic fibrosis and is linked to other negative health outcomes. Oral calorie supplements are often used to increase daily caloric intake and promote weight gain. However, these supplements are costly, and there are concerns that they may reduce regular food consumption without significantly improving overall energy intake. This study is an update of a previously published review. The objective of this review was to determine whether oral calorie supplements in individuals with cystic fibrosis can increase daily caloric intake, improve overall nutritional status, enhance nutritional indices, improve lung function, extend survival, and enhance quality of life. Additionally, the review aimed to assess any adverse effects associated with the use of these supplements. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, which includes references from electronic databases, hand-searched journals, and conference abstracts. They also contacted companies that market oral calorie supplements. The last search was conducted on October 18, 2016. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared the use of oral calorie supplements for at least one month to either no specific intervention or additional nutritional advice in individuals with cystic fibrosis. The researchers independently selected the trials, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted data. They also contacted the authors of the included trials to obtain additional information for two of the studies. Out of 21 identified trials, three were included in the review, involving a total of 131 participants. The duration of these trials ranged from three months to one year. Two trials compared oral calorie supplements to additional nutritional advice, while one trial compared supplements to no intervention. Two of the trials exclusively recruited children. One trial had a low risk of bias across all domains, while the other two had unclear or mixed risks of bias. In two trials, it was unclear whether participants were blinded, and in one trial, the clinical condition of the groups was unevenly balanced at baseline. Another trial raised concerns about allocation concealment. The results showed no significant differences between individuals receiving oral calorie supplements and those receiving dietary advice alone in terms of changes in weight, height, body mass index (BMI), z-scores, or other nutritional or growth indices. Specifically, changes in weight (in kilograms) at three, six, and 12 months were as follows: mean difference (MD) 0.32 (95% confidence interval [CI] -0.09 to 0.72), MD 0.47 (95% CI -0.07 to 1.02), and MD 0.16 (95% CI -0.68 to 1.00), respectively. However, total caloric intake was higher in individuals taking supplements at 12 months, with an MD of 265.70 (95% CI 42.94 to 488.46). There were no significant differences between the groups in terms of body composition, lung function, gastrointestinal adverse effects, or activity levels. The evidence for changes in weight and height was of moderate quality, while the evidence for changes in total caloric, fat, and protein intake was of low quality. This was because the results were only applicable to children aged 2 to 15 years, and many post-treatment diet diaries were not returned. Evidence regarding the rate of adverse events in the treatment groups was extremely limited and judged to be of very low quality. The authors concluded that oral calorie supplements do not provide additional benefits in the nutritional management of moderately malnourished children with cystic fibrosis beyond what can be achieved with dietary advice and monitoring alone. While nutritional supplements may be used, they should not be considered essential. Further randomized controlled trials are needed to clarify the role of short-term oral protein-energy supplements in individuals with cystic fibrosis experiencing acute weight loss, as well as their role in the long-term nutritional management of adults with cystic fibrosis or advanced lung disease.
